title: Episode 321: Queen Anne: Blenheim, the Duchess of Marlborough, the 1707 Act of Union, and the Sunset of the Stuarts

The monumental, sorrowful, and historic reign of Queen Anne, the last monarch of the House of Stuart. Suffering seventeen heartbreaking pregnancies with no surviving children, crippled by agonizing gout, Anne possessed an unshakeable devotion to the Church of England. Governing during the War of the Spanish Succession, her armies under John Churchill, Duke of Marlborough, won astounding victories at Blenheim, Ramillies, and Malplaquet. Tormented by an explosive, toxic falling-out with her lifelong favorite, Sarah Churchill, Anne presided over the historic 1707 Act of Union that created the United Kingdom of Great Britain. Discover the sovereign who united Britain.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series examines the last sovereign of the House of Stuart: a woman whose private life was an ocean of maternal grief, yet who forged the political union of Great Britain and vanquished the armies of France: Queen Anne. Here is George with the grand story of the first monarch of Great Britain.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: SEVENTEEN HEARTBREAKS: THE GRIEF OF PRINCESS ANNE: 1665 TO 1702
Born in February 1665 at St. James's Palace, Anne Stuart was the younger daughter of James, Duke of York, and Anne Hyde. Afflicted from childhood with defluxion of the eyes and chronic poor health, Anne was raised as a devout, unbending Anglican. In 1683, she made a comfortable, affectionate marriage to Prince George of Denmark, a handsome, phlegmatic prince whose quiet devotion anchored Anne's emotionally battered life. Yet Anne's domestic life was an unimaginable sequence of personal tragedy: between 1684 and 1700, Anne was pregnant seventeen times, suffering twelve miscarriages or stillbirths, while four infant children died within weeks of birth. Her only surviving child, Prince William, Duke of Gloucester, was born hydrocephalic with a swollen head; despite severe physical limitations, the boy was beloved by the entire nation as the great Protestant hope. In July 1700, days after his eleventh birthday party at Windsor Castle, little Prince William died suddenly of smallpox and scarlet fever. Anne knelt beside her dying son's bed in shattered silence, leaving the Stuart dynasty without a direct Protestant heir, forcing Parliament to pass the Act of Settlement. Anne's physical suffering was an agonizing backdrop to her entire adult life: her gout was so severe that she frequently could not bear even the weight of bedclothes upon her swollen limbs, and her eyes were constantly red and weeping from chronic rheum. Her Danish husband Prince George was a source of unwavering marital comfort, sitting by her couch for hours playing cards and holding her hand. When King Charles II had once remarked of George: 'I have tried him drunk, and I have tried him sober; and there is nothing in him', Anne fiercely defended her husband's kind, gentle loyalty against court mockery. Little Prince William's death left Anne spiritually devastated, but she bore her grief with stoic Christian dignity.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: MRS. MORLEY AND MRS. FREEMAN: THE MARLBOROUGH ALLIANCE
Anne's emotional anchor in a world of political hostility was Sarah Jennings, Duchess of Marlborough. From their girlhood in the Restoration court, Anne had fallen completely under the spell of Sarah's dazzling wit, radiant beauty, and fierce, domineering intellect. To escape the stifling formalities of royal etiquette, the two women adopted egalitarian pseudonyms in their extensive private correspondence: Anne was 'Mrs. Morley', while Sarah was 'Mrs. Freeman', writing to each other with passionate, intimate devotion. When Anne ascended the throne in March 1702 at age thirty-seven—so crippled by gout that she had to be carried to her Westminster coronation in an open sedan chair—she showered the Marlboroughs with astronomical wealth and power. Sarah was created Mistress of the Robes and Keeper of the Privy Purse, while her brilliant husband, John Churchill, was created Duke of Marlborough and Captain-General of all English and Allied forces in the War of the Spanish Succession. The relationship between 'Mrs. Morley' and 'Mrs. Freeman' was one of the most intense, psychologically complex female partnerships in British history. Sarah Churchill was brilliant, dazzlingly beautiful, and possessed a razor-sharp tongue that terrified courtiers, while Anne was quiet, shy, and emotionally needy. Sarah treated the Queen not as a sovereign, but as a submissive younger sister, correcting her grammar, managing her household, and dictating her political patronage. Yet as Anne grew into the responsibilities of the crown, she chafed under Sarah's relentless bullying, finding Sarah's violent Whig partisanship deeply offensive to her own heartfelt devotion to the Church of England.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE MIRACLE OF BLENHEIM: AUGUST 13, 1704
In the summer of 1704, King Louis XIV of France prepared to knock the Holy Roman Empire out of the war with a colossal French and Bavarian army advancing down the Danube River toward Vienna. In a breathtakingly audacious strategic march of two hundred and fifty miles across Germany in five weeks, Marlborough marched his English and Allied army from the Rhine to the Danube, keeping his destination secret even from his own allies. On August 13, 1704, near the Bavarian village of Blenheim, Marlborough and Prince Eugene of Savoy caught the combined Franco-Bavarian army under Marshal Tallard. In a day-long masterpiece of battlefield coordination, Marlborough pinned the French wings and launched eight thousand Allied cavalry in a thunderous charge across the Nebel stream, shattering the French center. Marshal Tallard was captured, twenty thousand French soldiers were killed or captured, and the myth of French invincibility was permanently broken. Marlborough penned a famous pencil note to Sarah on the back of a tavern bill: 'I have not time to say more, but to beg you will give my duty to the Queen, and let her know her army has had a glorious victory.' A grateful Queen Anne gifted Marlborough the royal manor of Woodstock and funded the construction of the colossal Baroque palace of Blenheim. Marlborough's march from Bedburg to the Danube in 1704 was a masterclass in military logistics and operational deception: he established supply depots along the route so his men were fed and shod daily, arriving in Bavaria in peak fighting condition while completely confounding French marshals. At Blenheim, Allied casualties were heavy—nearly twelve thousand men—but the destruction of the French army transformed Britain's international standing: for the first time since Agincourt, British infantry and cavalry had met the premier military superpower of continental Europe on an open field and smashed them to pieces. Queen Anne took immense personal pride in the victory, attending thanksgiving services in state and ordering the royal tapestries at Blenheim Palace.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE UNION OF 1707: THE BIRTH OF GREAT BRITAIN
Anne's crowning political achievement was the legislative union of England and Scotland. Since 1603, the two realms had shared a common monarch while retaining separate parliaments, legal systems, and economies. But following the economic collapse of the Darien Scheme and Scottish threats to choose a separate, non-Hanoverian monarch under the Act of Security, Anne recognized that political union was an existential necessity to prevent a hostile, French-allied kingdom on England's northern border. Anne passionately championed the Union, addressing both parliaments in person. Through brilliant diplomacy, economic incentives—including English assumption of Scotland's national debt through the 'Equivalent' fund—and free access to England's vast colonial trading empire, the Treaty of Union was ratified. On May 1, 1707, the Parliament of Scotland held its final session, with Chancellor James Ogilvy sadly declaring: 'Now there's ane end of ane old song.' The kingdoms of England and Scotland were united into a single, sovereign realm: the Kingdom of Great Britain. Anne attended a magnificent Thanksgiving service at St. Paul's Cathedral, hailed as the first Queen of Great Britain. The Scottish opposition to the Treaty of Union was fierce and tumultuous: anti-Union riots rocked Edinburgh and Glasgow, copies of the treaty were publicly burned, and Scottish poet Robert Burns would later lament that the Scottish nobility had been 'bought and sold for English gold'. Yet the economic reality was inescapable: Scotland gained unhindered access to the expanding markets of England and the American colonies, while preserving its distinct Presbyterian Kirk, its unique Scottish legal system based on Roman law, and its ancient Scottish universities. Queen Anne considered the Union the grandest achievement of her reign, declaring to Parliament that she desired nothing more than that all her subjects should be united in hearts and affection.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE ROYAL FALL-OUT: ABIGAIL MASHAM AND THE FALL OF SARAH CHURCHILL: 1708 TO 1711
While British armies won further victories at Ramillies, Oudenarde, and Malplaquet, the intimate friendship between Anne and Sarah Churchill soured into poisonous hatred. Sarah was an aggressive, outspoken Whig who browbeat the queen into appointing Whig ministers, mocking Anne's devout high-church Anglican piety and treating the monarch with insolent condescension. Seeking warmth, sympathy, and quiet deference, Queen Anne found solace in her impoverished cousin, Abigail Masham, a gentle bedchamber woman whom Sarah had originally introduced to court. When Sarah discovered that Abigail was secretly meeting the Queen and acting as a backchannel for Tory politician Robert Harley, Sarah's fury exploded. In a sensational public confrontation at St. Paul's Cathedral in August 1708, Sarah ordered the Queen to 'Be quiet!' in full view of the congregation. In April 1710, the two women held their final, devastating meeting at Kensington Palace: Sarah wept and raged, demanding an explanation, while Anne coldly repeated: 'I shall make you no other answer than what I gave you: put it in writing.' The Marlboroughs were stripped of all royal offices, and Sarah was banished from court forever. Abigail Masham's quiet, soothing deference was the perfect antidote to Sarah Churchill's abrasive temper. While Sarah hectored and scolded, Abigail brewed tea, conversed gently, and listened patiently to the ailing queen's complaints. When Sarah discovered the secret influence Abigail held through Harley, Sarah's jealousy degenerated into vicious personal attacks, spreading scurrilous rumors that Anne and Abigail engaged in an unnatural, lesbian relationship. This grotesque slander destroyed any lingering affection Anne felt for Sarah. When Anne finally demanded Sarah surrender her golden key of office as Mistress of the Robes, the furious Duchess threw the key onto the floor in a fit of rage, severing their thirty-year friendship forever.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE TREATY OF UTRECHT AND THE TORY MINISTRY: 1711 TO 1713
With the Marlboroughs disgraced, Anne appointed a Tory ministry headed by Robert Harley and Henry St. John, Viscount Bolingbroke, determined to bring an end to the ruinously expensive European war. When the Whig-dominated House of Lords threatened to block peace negotiations, Anne executed an unprecedented constitutional maneuver in December 1711: she created twelve new hereditary Tory peers in a single day—including Abigail Masham's husband—to pack the Lords and secure a peace majority. In April 1713, Great Britain signed the historic Treaty of Utrecht, concluding the War of the Spanish Succession. The treaty was an astonishing imperial triumph for Britain: Louis XIV recognized the Protestant Hanoverian succession, while Britain acquired Gibraltar, Minorca, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, and the highly lucrative Asiento monopoly to supply enslaved Africans to the Spanish Empire. Great Britain emerged from the war as the undisputed preeminent maritime and commercial superpower of the world. The creation of twelve Tory peers in 1711 was a radical constitutional assertion of the royal prerogative that stunned the House of Lords. When the twelve new lords took their seats, the Whig peer Lord Wharton mockingly asked them whether they intended to vote by their foreman, as if they were a common jury. Yet the peace of Utrecht laid the foundations of the British Empire for the next two centuries: the acquisition of Gibraltar and Minorca gave the Royal Navy absolute command of the Mediterranean, while the Asiento slave contract enriched British merchants in Bristol and Liverpool, catapulting the City of London into the financial capital of the globe.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE BROKEN FRAME AND THE END OF THE STUARTS: AUGUST 1714
Anne's final months were an agonizing ordeal of physical decay and vicious political infighting between Harley and Bolingbroke. Suffering from massive obesity, severe gout, and recurring erysipelas, the forty-nine-year-old queen was unable to walk and plagued by fevers. On July 27, 1714, after a grueling Privy Council meeting that lasted until two in the morning, Anne collapsed in exhaustion. Two days later, she suffered a catastrophic stroke at Kensington Palace. In a final, lucid moment of statecraft on July 30, Anne handed the White Staff of Lord Treasurer to Charles Talbot, Duke of Shrewsbury, gasping: 'Use it for the good of my people', securing the peaceful succession for the Protestant House of Hanover. On the morning of Sunday, August 1, 1714, Queen Anne died. Her body was so swollen that she had to be buried in Westminster Abbey in a colossal, almost square coffin. With Anne's death, the House of Stuart came to an end after one hundred and eleven years, passing the British throne to fifty-four-year-old George, Elector of Hanover. On her deathbed at Kensington Palace, as Harley and Bolingbroke traded savage recriminations across her bedchamber, Anne showed remarkable fortitude. By conferring the Lord Treasurer's staff upon the Duke of Shrewsbury—a moderate Protestant magnate—Anne ensured that the Jacobite faction could not stage a coup to restore her exiled Catholic half-brother. Her death marked the end of the romantic, tragic Stuart century that had witnessed civil war, regicide, republic, and restoration. Queen Anne had presided over an era of profound cultural brilliance—the age of Jonathan Swift, Alexander Pope, Daniel Defoe, and Sir Isaac Newton—leaving behind a united and victorious Great Britain poised to become a global titan.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for joining us for this episode of Most Fascinating Stories. If you enjoyed this chapter of Queen Anne: Blenheim, the Duchess of Marlborough, the 1707 Act of Union, and the Sunset of the Stuarts, subscribe to the show, share it with a fellow history lover, and tune in next Tuesday for our next journey into history's most extraordinary events. Until next time, I'm Rebecca.
